extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency officials, judges, regulatory practitioners, and interest-group attorneys involved in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and reform-oriented criteria for producing, managing, and reviewing information in administrative notice-and-comment rulemakings to prevent 'information capture' and 'filter failure.' Covers participant filing practices, agency process design, and judicial review norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information capture (definition and warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information capture: the excessive use of information and related information costs as a means of gaining control over regulatory decisionmaking in informal rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a continuous barrage of letters, telephone calls, meetings, memoranda, formal comments, post-rule comments, petitions for reconsideration, and notices of appeal that produce a 'machine-gun' effect on overstretched agency staff; results in a lopsided administrative record and domination of the agenda by well-resourced stakeholders. Use this concept to evaluate whether submissions are being wielded strategically to dominate the record rather than to illuminate issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter failure (participants should self-process information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filter failure: absence of requirements that participants process and hone the information they communicate to agencies, leading to excessive, undigested, or strategic filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts administrative process with courts/trials that impose page/time/evidence limits; recommends recognizing that participants bear responsibility to distill and prioritize information they submit rather than offloading processing costs onto agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undigested, redundant, peripheral materials in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should not consist of undigested facts, redundancies, peripheral issues, or overly intricate details of trivial significance that inflate processing costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and cull redundancies and peripheral materials; avoid pitching discussions at too specialized a level or demanding unreasonable background knowledge from readers. These forms of excess increase the cost of participation and skew pluralistic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise general statement requirement (agency rulemaking statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required by the APA to provide a 'concise general statement of their basis and purpose' for a rule, but courts often enforce this as requiring more detail rather than concision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforce the statutory adjectives 'concise' and 'general' (rather than judicially preferred 'detailed' and 'encyclopedic') so agencies avoid loading rules and records with excessive detail merely to survive judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate judicial review to robustness of pluralistic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recalibrate judicial review to focus on the process (robustness of pluralistic participation) rather than on the substantive detail contributed by single dominant commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed scheme: grant considerable deference (a 'soft glance') when diverse, balanced participation is present; presume against challengers when one party dominates rulemaking (affording more deference to the agency); and afford a hard look where underrepresented groups were excluded. Courts need rules for measuring imbalance and may add a good-faith requirement to petitions to limit strategic abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and documentation required to preserve issues under current law
rubrics_metrics.description: Under current jurisprudence, commenters generally must file specific, detailed, well-documented comments during notice-and-comment to preserve issues for later litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that this rule incentivizes voluminous, highly specific submissions ('build the best record') and thus contributes to information excess; when drafting comments for litigation purposes, include concrete evidence and argumentation rather than general objections, but be mindful of the information-cost tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose page/volume/format limits on filings (information filters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts or agencies should impose simple filters—page limits, volume restrictions, formatting rules—on filings to force participants to control information excess at the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to appellate page limits and trial-time limits; courts could scrutinize comments for clarity and accessibility; limits will not eliminate specialized material but will encourage succinctness and prioritize the most important issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require verification of data and supporting analysis for critical assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should be required to verify the reliability of data presented and to provide supporting analysis for critical factual assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This filter would help agencies and courts focus on substantive, reliable evidence rather than undigested data dumps; could include sworn attestations, methodologies, or citations to underlying data to prevent informational gamesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency ombudsmen/advocates/advisory review to reinvigorate pluralistic engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy government intermediaries (agency-selected ombudsmen, advocates, advisory groups, or ALJs) to stand in for interests likely to be underrepresented in rulemakings and to ensure agencies consider broader values (e.g., public health).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ombudsmen would scrutinize rules, file comments, build records, and bring missing perspectives into the administrative record. Expert advisory committees could review highly technical rules to ensure missing affected interests are considered; their opinions could be part of the record subject to agency response and judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidize participation by thinly financed groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide subsidies, prizes, competitions, or other rewards to increase participation by underfunded public-interest groups in complex rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms include monetary prizes for meaningful public-benefitting comments, law school competitions, fee-shifting or standing for winners to litigate on behalf of winning submissions. These incentives lower participation costs and improve pluralistic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add procedural filters analogous to trial/evidentiary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Import filtering concepts from other legal settings (e.g., limits on pages/margins/font, FR Evid-type exclusions) so that the parties, rather than the agency, bear processing costs before material is introduced into the administrative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use filters to ensure submissions have passed some adversarial or evidentiary refinement; courts and agencies could refuse to consider undisciplined or non-evidentiary mass filings that are unlikely to aid informed decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid agencies gathering decision-relevant information outside formal notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not retreat to gathering information outside established notice-and-comment channels as a coping strategy for information overload, because that reduces transparency and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage off-the-record consultations or ex post nontransparent adjustments to rules; keep the deliberative process within public procedures and improve those procedures rather than bypass them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-in-the-raw: insulated pre-proposal development
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a two-step process where a small, insulated agency team develops a detailed, accessible pre-proposal (policy-in-the-raw) free from stakeholder pressures, followed by peer review (non-stakeholder) and subsequent public engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pre-proposal stage enables more candid, innovative analysis and alternatives assessment without litigation pressures; publish pre-proposal and reviewers' comments; agency may adopt or disregard peer input without fear of judicial reprimand for not adopting stakeholder-driven changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition-based regulation to scramble incentives among regulated parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Design procedures that encourage regulated parties to challenge competitors (e.g., petitions by greener manufacturers against inferior products) so market actors surface valuable information and focus attention on the worst products/processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adjudicatory hearings initiated by competitors, letting market rivalry triage regulatory attention and surface contestable factual information that otherwise might be buried in undigested filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize doctrinal incentives (hard look; substantial evidence) that encourage defensive overkill
rubrics_metrics.description: Current doctrines—hard look review and occasional demands for substantial evidence—create incentives for agencies (and commenters) to engage in defensive overkill by loading the record with excessive detail to ward off judicial reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating agency rules or designing reforms, account for these incentives and consider reforms (e.g., recalibrated review standards) that reduce the need for agencies to fill records defensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion and materiality rules shape comment drafting incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines requiring exhaustion of administrative remedies and treating general comments as legally immaterial push stakeholders to file highly specific, well-documented comments during the notice-and-comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that these doctrines, while intended to preserve issues for litigation and conserve resources, also intensify information excess; reforms should balance the need to preserve issues with limits that avoid encouraging data-dumps.
